title: Mirror, Mirror, in the Tank: Octopuses Learn to Use Reflections to Hunt
summary: Octopuses are already famous escape artists and puzzle solvers, but new research reveals a skill that puts them in an even more exclusive club. Scientists at Dartmouth College have shown that octopuses can learn to use mirrors to find food they cannot see directly—a cognitive feat previously documented only in some mammals and birds. The study, published in Current Biology, is the first to demonstrate mirror-guided spatial reasoning in an invertebrate. The team worked with three California two-spot octopuses in a specially designed tank. First, the animals were given time to acclimate to a mirror placed in their habitat. Then came the crucial training phase: a live crab was sealed inside a glass jar positioned so the octopus could see it only through the mirror. To reach the snack, the octopus had to turn 90 degrees and navigate around a corner. “We don’t enter the world knowing how to use a mirror but learn how to use a mirror,” explains senior author Peter Tse, a cognitive neuroscientist at Dartmouth. “Octopuses can also learn how to use a mirror to infer where things are in the world.” To rule out the possibility that the animals were simply following chemical cues, the researchers switched to a virtual crab image during formal testing. Each octopus was placed in a start box with a mirror directly in front. The virtual crab appeared behind the octopus, on either its left or right side, visible only in the reflection. To earn a real crab reward, the octopus had to recognize the image’s true location and move toward it—not toward the mirror itself. Remarkably, the octopuses learned to do exactly that. Some even climbed over the side of the box instead of swimming around it, shaving seconds off their time. While they didn’t always take the shortest path, their speed improved significantly across trials. The implications stretch beyond cephalopod trivia. Octopuses are among the most evolutionarily distant animals from humans; our last common ancestor was a worm that lived 350 to 500 million years ago. “Given that such a remote organism has independently evolved the means to use a mirror as a tool to process spatial cognition suggests that the underlying cognitive processes might be subject to convergent evolution,” says lead author Mary Kieseler. In other words, nature may have arrived at similar neural solutions to the same problem more than once. The researchers suspect this ability is tied to the octopus’s hunting style. Like cats, octopuses sneak up on prey and pounce, a strategy that benefits from an internal mental map of the environment. “Our work suggests that octopuses might also have internal maps, an internal representation of space,” Tse says. More research is needed to confirm that hypothesis, but the study already adds a dazzling new entry to the octopus’s résumé of extraordinary talents.
why_it_matters: The study's finding that complex spatial reasoning can evolve in animals with such different brains could reshape our understanding of intelligence across the tree of life and even guide the design of flexible, brain-inspired robots.

background_read: Mirror tests have fascinated scientists for decades; a few smart animals, like chimpanzees (our closest relatives), bottlenose dolphins, and Eurasian magpies, can recognize their own reflection.

Octopuses, though, are invertebrates with a completely different brain design — a distributed nervous system where many neurons are in their arms — yet they have amazed researchers by opening child-proof jars and solving mazes.

The new experiment, conducted at Dartmouth College (a private US university in New Hampshire), led by cognitive neuroscientist Peter Tse and researcher Mary Kieseler, targeted a different skill: using a mirror to locate hidden prey.
They published their findings in Current Biology, a well-known scientific journal, after work with three California two-spot octopuses, a species found along the Pacific coast of North America.

Because the last common ancestor of octopuses and humans lived around 400 million years ago — a flatworm-like creature — the appearance of such an ability in octopuses suggests that nature hit upon similar solutions twice through convergent evolution.
This discovery could influence how we think about intelligence in other distant lifeforms, including potential alien intelligences.

perspectives.description: This research highlights the remarkable cognitive abilities of octopuses, showing they can solve problems in ways previously thought limited to mammals. It opens new doors for understanding how intelligence can emerge in different nervous systems, possibly inspiring more sophisticated artificial intelligence.

With only three octopuses tested, the sample size is small, and some experts might argue that the behavior could be a form of simple association learning rather than true mirror-based spatial reasoning. The laboratory setup also doesn't fully replicate natural conditions.

The study contributes to the concept of convergent evolution by demonstrating that a cognitive trait, often tied to complex brains, appears in an invertebrate. This raises fundamental questions: what are the minimum neural circuits required for such skills, and how many times did they independently arise?

Future experiments with larger sample sizes and different octopus species could establish this ability as a regular feature of cephalopod cognition. If confirmed, it may encourage the search for mirror use in other invertebrates and influence how we test intelligence in non-mammalian life, including robotic systems.
